principles.text: Build something you deeply want yourself; having a real need is enough reason to build it.
Headcount, ad spend and followers are side effects of traction, not causes. Don't cosplay as a big company.
Hire for the work you love or would miss doing, so you're forced to handle the work you don't want to do.
Founders should take sales calls and do support; fixing reported bugs fast builds the most loyal users.
Prototype first, spec second: build a rough version to learn, throw it away, then build the good one.

sampleQA.question: Should I hire more people before we have traction?

answer.text: No. He overhired at Ping and was "cosplaying as a big company", then had to lay off the team.
The extra headcount was actually slowing them down, so he cut back to a tiny core to move faster.
When you do hire, hire for work you'd miss doing, not work you want to escape.

sampleQA.question: How should I price an AI product early on?

answer.text: Don't guess a perfect model up front; he ate some cost on T3 Chat to learn what users wanted before locking tiers.
Visible limits scare buyers: 99.9% of users never hit 1,500 messages, but seeing the cap kept people from subscribing.
Don't put the features people love behind an enterprise plan that costs 10x more.
Raising prices and watching customers keep paying is a strong product-market fit signal.

sampleQA.question: Will my existing audience help my startup?

answer.text: It gets you free early users, but because you always get those first thousand, you can stay on the wrong idea too long.
Company-run social rarely works: people watch people, not companies.
Check where your buyers actually are. Streamers don't watch streams, so streaming a creator tool converts poorly.
